title: Graph Paper
blurb: Classic square-grid graph paper for math, plotting functions, drawing charts, and pixel or bullet-journal layouts. The default 1/4-inch grid is the size most school worksheets and quad notebooks use.
tip: Switch to 5 mm or 1/5 inch for tighter plots, or 1 cm for roomier graphing. Turn the margin on if you plan to hole-punch or bind the sheet.

title: Grid Paper
blurb: Plain square grid paper — the same even squares as graph paper, defaulting to a metric 5 mm grid that suits engineering rough work, tiling and floor-plan sketches, and cross-stitch or perler-bead patterns.
tip: Pick 1 cm squares for quick scale drawings, or drop to 1/8 inch when you need fine detail. Black or blue lines photocopy more cleanly than gray.

title: Dot Grid Paper
blurb: Dot grid paper places a small dot at each grid intersection instead of full lines, so your own writing and drawing stay the star. It is the standard for bullet journaling, hand-lettering guides, and clean diagrams.
tip: 5 mm dots match most bullet-journal notebooks; 1/4 inch gives more breathing room. Light gray dots nearly vanish once you write over them.

title: Dot Paper
blurb: Dot paper is a spaced grid of dots used for dots-and-boxes games, geoboard and array math, and lettering practice. The wider 1/4-inch default keeps the dots easy to connect by hand.
tip: For the classic dots-and-boxes game, print at 1/4 inch and play on a portrait sheet. Choose a darker line color if you are photocopying for a class.

title: Isometric Paper
blurb: Isometric paper is a triangular grid — vertical lines crossed by two sets of 30-degree diagonals — for drawing 3D objects, isometric game maps, and packaging or product sketches without a ruler.
tip: Draw box edges along the three line directions and cubes come out in true isometric perspective. Smaller spacing packs in more detail for complex builds.

title: Hexagonal Paper
blurb: Hex paper tiles the page with even hexagons — the standard for tabletop and wargame maps, organic chemistry ring structures, and hex-based board game design.
tip: Larger hexes suit game maps you will draw terrain into; smaller hexes fit chemistry chains. One hex equals one map tile at any size you choose.

title: Engineering Paper
blurb: Engineering paper uses a fine grid with a heavier line every fifth square, so you can sketch to scale and still read whole units at a glance. Traditional pads print the grid faintly on the back — work goes on the plain front and the grid shows through.
tip: The default 1/10-inch grid with a bold 1/2-inch major line is the classic green engineering-pad layout. Print single-sided for a working front, or use it grid-side up for graphing.

title: Lined Paper
blurb: Lined writing paper with a colored left margin. Choose your ruling: wide ruled (11/32 inch) for younger writers, college ruled (9/32 inch) for everyday note-taking, or narrow ruled (1/4 inch) to fit more lines per page.
tip: College ruled fits about 33 lines on a Letter page; wide ruled fits about 25. Switch the ruling above and the line spacing updates before you print.

title: Handwriting Paper
blurb: Handwriting practice paper with a solid top line, a dashed midline, and a solid baseline in each row — the guide young writers use to size and place letters correctly for print and early cursive.
tip: Letters like a and e sit between the midline and baseline; tall letters reach the top line. Larger row heights suit beginners; drop to the smaller size as handwriting matures.

title: Cornell Notes Paper
blurb: The Cornell note-taking template: a narrow left cue column for questions and keywords, a wide right column for notes, and a summary band across the bottom. A proven layout for lectures and active review.
tip: Take notes in the right column during class, add cue questions on the left afterward, then write a one- or two-line summary at the bottom to lock in recall.

title: Music Staff Paper
blurb: Blank music manuscript paper — evenly spaced five-line staves for writing melodies, exercises, and lead sheets by hand. No clefs or time signatures are printed, so it works for any instrument or key.
tip: Larger staff spacing gives more room for note heads and lyrics; smaller spacing fits more staves per page for dense scores. Landscape suits wide piano systems.
